stories.headline: Which NBA deals will get done? Bobby Marks' biggest extension decisions to watch
stories.summary: With Monday's extension deadline looming, Bobby Marks breaks down the biggest decisions around the league.
stories.body:
The NBA season starts in one week, but that isn't the only thing on the minds of league executives. The deadline for rookie extensions is Monday, a day before the 2026-27 regular season tips off.

Since the start of the offseason, five players -- Victor Wembanyama, Amen and Ausar Thompson, Keyonte George and Brandin Podziemski -- have signed rookie extensions. That's currently far below the average of 11 rookie extensions signed per year since 2023, but expect that number to rise in the coming days. Of the 34 players to land rookie extensions in the past three seasons, 17 signed on deadline day.

What deals will the next week bring? We broke down what to expect for six of the 16 eligible players.

Rookie extension decisions aren't the only things we're watching. Oct. 19 is also the deadline to extend veterans with two years remaining on their contract -- not including an option year -- and the deadline to reduce rosters to 15 players on standard contracts.

Let's examine the league's most important extension decisions and what Monday's deadline could bring for teams around the league.

Jump to a section:

Six big rookie extension decisions

KAT, Giannis among vets to watch

Moves coming for Lakers, Knicks?

Rookie extension candidates to watch

Brandon Miller, Charlotte Hornets
Why an extension could get done: Following offseason trades of LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges, the Hornets view Miller and Kon Knueppel as the franchise's new foundation. An injury-plagued sophomore 2024-25 season limited Miller to 27 games, but he rebounded last season to post career highs in 3-pointers made, 3-point percentage and free throw attempts and averaged more than 20 points per game for the second straight season.

Why it might not: Miller views Amen Thompson's five-year, $208 million extension with Houston as a comparable salary. The main difference: Thompson played at least 60 games in each of his first three seasons and was selected for the All-Defensive First Team in 2025.

What I would offer: Five years, $175 million. The contract can either start at $30.2 million and increase each year, ending at $39.8 million, or start high and decline each season. (Coby White's latest contract with the Hornets declines in Years 2 and 3.) With no player earning more than $25 million in 2027-28, Charlotte has the flexibility to increase Miller's offer. Not including new contracts for Miller and center Moussa Diabate, who is eligible for an extension in February, Charlotte projects to be $80 million under the luxury tax next season.

Dereck Lively II, Dallas Mavericks

Why an extension could get done: The Mavericks would need to bypass injury concerns and look at his impact when healthy. Despite playing only 36 games in 2024-25, Lively ranked 17th out of 138 players in offensive rebounding percentage and fourth in defensive rebounding percentage. During that season, Lively held opponents to 56.3% of shooting at the rim, ranking 20th out of 165 players. In 21 postseason games as a rookie, Lively averaged 7.4 rebounds in 22 minutes per game.

Why it might not: What else? Injuries and durability. Lively has played a total of 98 games in his first three seasons, including 55 his rookie year, and missed all but seven games last season. He had right foot surgery in July 2025 before another surgery on the same foot four months later. Lively continues to ramp up his recovery but was not cleared to play 5-on-5 during training camp.

What I would offer: Three years, $35 million. The first-year, $10.8 million salary is comparable to the one-year qualifying offer Lively is eligible for next summer if an extension is not reached. The second year is guaranteed, but the third is contingent on Lively playing at least 41 games in the first or second season of the contract.

Jaime Jaquez Jr., Milwaukee Bucks

Why an extension could get done: If we are evaluating Jaquez off last season with Miami, then discussions for a new contract are warranted. With the Heat, Jaquez became one of four players to average at least 15 points, five rebounds and four assists off the bench since the 1982-83 season. The forward shot a career-high 50.7% last season and saw his assists nearly double from 2.5 to 4.7. Considering Kyle Kuzma is on an expiring contract and Nate Ament is in his rookie season, having Jaquez under contract should be a priority.

Why it might not: Other than failing to reach a compromise, Milwaukee could pause extension talks to evaluate how Jaquez fits in with new Bucks coach Taylor Jenkins.

What I would offer: Four years, $78.8 million. Comparable to Jaquez's free agent hold, the contract starts at $17.8 million and ends with a player option.

Cason Wallace, Oklahoma City Thunder
Why an extension could get done: If there ever was an indication, it was the trade sending Lu Dort to Atlanta.

"I would just say Cason is someone we think very highly of and has done a great job for us," Thunder general manager Sam Presti said before training camp. "I think the greatest sign of respect we could have shown Cason is moving Lu [Dort] in that trade. We potentially could have looked at a series of other options, but it's a bit of a gesture to him to say, 'We think you can have a great role on this team. We believe in you as a player.'"

Named All-Defense for the first time in his career, Wallace led all players in steals last season. He finished seventh in Defensive Player of the Year voting and was one of five guards (Dyson Daniels, Derrick White, Andrew Nembhard, Amen Thompson) over the past two seasons to win Defensive Player of the Month.

Why it might not: Second apron concerns. With Year 1 of Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's supermax extension beginning, Oklahoma City is $1.9 million over the second apron. A contract for Wallace starting at $25 million not only puts the Thunder deeper into the apron but will cost them an additional $150 million in luxury taxes. As this past offseason proved with the trades of Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe, Oklahoma City is not afraid to make difficult choices to keep its core intact.

What I would offer: Five years, $145 million. The contract starts at $25 million and increases to $33 million in the final year. You can make a case that Wallace should get more in guaranteed money than Keyonte George and Ausar Thompson, but Oklahoma City is in a different bracket financially than Utah and Detroit.

Anthony Black, Orlando Magic
Why an extension could get done: Past precedent. The Magic have been aggressive in signing former draft picks to rookie extensions. In the past three offseasons, Orlando has extended Cole Anthony, Jalen Suggs, Franz Wagner and Paolo Banchero. If not for injuring his back in early March, Black would have been a candidate for 2026 Most Improved Player; his scoring increased from 9.4 to 15.3 points per game and he shot a career-high 44.7% from the field. Defensively, Black had 25 games with multiple steals.

Why it might not: Finances. A new contract would likely put Orlando over the luxury tax for consecutive seasons and over the first apron. The Magic are a projected $20 million under the tax threshold. Next season and in 2028-29, they will have four players (Wagner, Banchero, Desmond Bane, Jalen Suggs) earning more than $26 million. Considering Orlando has failed to advance past the first round with this roster, is it prudent to pay a significant penalty once again?

What I would offer: There are two ways to look at Black's next contract: the deal Orlando should offer because of its financial constraints, and what Black deserves. If the goal is to remain below the luxury tax, the starting salary cannot exceed $13 million -- below the $16 million non-tax midlevel exception for next season. There is also the question of whether Orlando views him as a starter or a sixth man. The starting backcourt of Suggs and Bane is under contract through at least the 2028-29 season.

Scoot Henderson, Portland Trail Blazers
Why an extension could get done: The Trail Blazers view Henderson's production in the first round of the playoffs as a reason to lock up the former No. 3 pick to a long-term contract. In the first three games against the Spurs, Henderson scored 70 points. Over the past 30 seasons, only Brandon Roy (82 points in 2009) and Damian Lillard (79 points in 2014) scored more through their first three playoﬀ games as a Blazer.

Why it might not: Other than a small sample in the playoffs, what has Henderson done in his first three seasons to show he is worthy of a lucrative contract? Henderson's career field goal percentage (40.4%) is the second worst of any player in the past three seasons. And on defense, Henderson allowed 51.4% shooting from the field as the closest defender last season. Also, how does Henderson fit with new coach Micah Nori and a crowded backcourt of Lillard, Jrue Holiday and Ja Morant?

What I would offer: Three years, $51.8 million. The first-year salary of $16 million is comparable to the non-tax midlevel exception.

Other players eligible for rookie extensions: Noah Clowney (Brooklyn), Julian Strawther (Denver), Marcus Sasser (Dallas), Ben Sheppard (Indiana), Jarace Walker (Indiana), Gradey Dick (LA Clippers), Taylor Hendricks (Memphis), Kris Murray (Memphis), Brice Sensabaugh (Utah), Bilal Coulibaly (Washington)

Veteran extension candidates

Recent extensions for Kawhi Leonard and Stephen Curry have continued the trend of stars choosing guaranteed money over hitting free agency. Since the offseason started in July, 11 potential free agents extended their contracts, including Leonard, Curry and Donovan Mitchell.

There are two sets of deadlines for players who are extension-eligible. For players with two years or more remaining on their contract, such as the Celtics' Payton Pritchard, Monday is the deadline to extend. Players with one year remaining on their contract have until June 30 to extend.

If a player has two years left on his contract but with an option in the last season, however, he is also eligible to extend up to June 30. This group includes Nikola Jokic, Karl-Anthony Towns, Giannis Antetokounmpo and Anthony Davis. For each of the four players to extend after Oct. 19, the player option must be eliminated and replaced with the first year of the extension.

Here are where things stand ahead of that Oct. 19 deadline:

Nikola Jokic, Denver Nuggets
For the second consecutive offseason, Jokic will not sign an extension in Denver. The lack of long-term security has nothing to do with his unhappiness in Denver, but rather his ability to maximize finances next offseason. By waiting until the 2027 offseason, Jokic is eligible to sign a five-year, $359.5 million contract as a free agent. That contract would be the largest in NBA history and see his career on-court earnings reach $724 million.

Karl-Anthony Towns, New York Knicks

Towns has repeatedly said the goal is to get a new contract done with New York.

"Simply put, I want to do something that can keep the team together and work with the Knicks and also values me," Towns said on Oct. 5. The Knicks are thinking differently, stating they will not negotiate any extensions until later in the season.

Since the NBA Finals concluded in mid-June, Towns has been eligible to sign up to a four-year, $276 million extension. Talks have reached an impasse, per Towns, however. "None of those things have come close to happening," he said.

The holdup on why New York is not writing a blank check comes down to second apron concerns over the foreseeable future. With Towns' $61 million player option in 2027-28, New York is likely to exceed the second apron. They are currently $9 million below the threshold and have five open roster spots. The purse strings get even tighter in the summer of 2028.

Not including new contracts for Towns and Josh Hart and a significant raise for Jalen Brunson (his salary will likely increase from $43.3 to $64.7 million), New York will project to be $104 million below the second apron.

For example, if New York signed Towns to a four-year, $227 million extension ($53 million, $57.4 million, $61.5 million and $65.7 million), extended Hart starting at $20 million and signed Brunson to a max contract, it guarantees New York as a second apron team for the 2028-29 season. Knicks owner James Dolan said after the Finals that New York will not exceed the second apron.

Giannis Antetokounmpo, Miami Heat
Antetokounmpo has been extension-eligible since Oct. 1 but at considerably less money because he was traded on July 6. The extension would be either three years, $194 million or two years, $135.1 million. But waiting until Jan. 6 (six months after the trade) would make Antetokounmpo eligible to sign a four-year, $276 million extension. The $62.8 million player option would be replaced with Year 1 of the extension.

One scenario not to be overlooked: Antetokounmpo mirroring Jokic and re-signing with Miami as a free agent in the 2027 offseason. By not extending in January, Antetokounmpo would then become eligible for a five-year, $357 million contract. His potential $754 million in career on court earnings would be the most in NBA history.

Anthony Davis, Washington Wizards

Do not expect a Davis extension in the near future.

"[I'll decide] when the season is over," Davis said on media day. "We're going to go through the season and try to do what I do at a high level. ... And then when it's over, sit down and have those conversations again with the front office."

Davis became eligible to sign an extension in early August for up to four years and $275 million. He holds a player option for $62 million next season, the final year of a three-year, $175 million deal he signed with the Lakers. The first year of an extension would replace that player option. Davis, 33, did not play with Washington after he was acquired at last season's trade deadline, and he has failed to reach 60 games in five of the past six seasons.

Jaden McDaniels, Minnesota Timberwolves

McDaniels is eligible to extend for two years and $87 million. (Because he has three years remaining on his current contract, the first year of the extension would not start until 2029-30.) Last season, McDaniels increased his scoring from 14.8 points per game in the regular season to 16.5 in the playoffs and scored a season-high 32 points in the Game 6 clincher against Denver. In that series, McDaniels also held All-Star Jamal Murray to 32% shooting as the closest defender.

More players to watch

Oct. 19 deadline: Onyeka Okongwu (Atlanta), Terance Mann (Brooklyn), Royce O'Neale (Charlotte), Nicolas Claxton (Chicago), Moses Moody (Golden State), Pascal Siakam (Indiana), Obi Toppin (Indiana), Andrew Nembhard (Indiana), Tyrese Haliburton (Indiana), Ivica Zubac (Indiana), Darius Garland (LA Clippers), Anthony Edwards (Minnesota), LaMelo Ball (Minnesota), Jaden McDaniels (Minnesota), Karlo Matkovic (New Orleans), Zion Williamson (New Orleans), Desmond Bane (Orlando), Jaylen Brown (Philadelphia), Deni Avdija (Portland), Ja Morant (Portland), Domantas Sabonis (Sacramento), Devin Vassell (San Antonio).

June 30 deadline: Lu Dort (Atlanta), Mouhamed Gueye (Atlanta), Paul George (Boston), Michael Porter Jr. (Brooklyn), Grant Williams (Charlotte), Leonard Miller (Chicago), Jalen Smith (Chicago), Isaac Okoro (Chicago), Buddy Hield (Chicago), Craig Porter Jr. (Cleveland), Max Christie (Dallas), Caleb Martin (Dallas), Cameron Johnson (Denver), Zeke Nnaji (Denver), Johnny Furphy (Indiana), Jay Huff (Indiana), Kris Dunn (LA Clippers), Derrick Jones Jr. (LA Clippers), Cam Christie (LA Clippers), Max Strus (LA Clippers), Jarred Vanderbilt (LA Lakers), Bronny James (LA Lakers), Jaden Hardy (LA Lakers), Isaiah Stewart (Memphis), Jaylen Wells (Memphis), Scotty Pippen Jr. (Memphis), Jerami Grant (Memphis), Giannis Antetokounmpo (Miami), Kyle Kuzma (Milwaukee), Tyler Herro (Milwaukee), Donte DiVincenzo (Minnesota), Rudy Gobert (Minnesota), Jordan Poole (New Orleans), Dejounte Murray (New Orleans), Josh Hart (New York), Tyler Kolek (New York), Miles McBride (New York), Goga Bitadze (Orlando), Adem Bona (Philadelphia), Jalen Green (Phoenix), Oso Ighodaro (Phoenix), Miles Bridges (Phoenix), Vit Krejci (Portland), Zach LaVine (Sacramento), De'Andre Hunter (Sacramento), Malik Monk (Sacramento), Keldon Johnson (San Antonio), Kyle Filopowski (Utah), Svi Mykhailiuk (Utah).

Key roster decisions around the league

Nearly 80 players will hit waivers Saturday night in anticipation of Monday's deadline to cut rosters to 15 players. Teams will incur a per-day cap hit if a player signed to a non-guaranteed contract is not waived by 5 p.m. ET on Saturday. For example, the Knicks would be charged $17,622 per day against the cap if James Wiseman is not waived by Saturday. New York is currently over the luxury tax and first apron. The full salary counts against the apron.

Here are three more teams to watch as the Monday roster deadline approaches:

Los Angeles Lakers
Is there a trade on the horizon to consolidate the Lakers' roster? With 16 players currently on guaranteed contracts, Los Angeles will need to open up a roster spot either in a trade or by releasing a player.

"Behind that evaluation of who's emerging in camp, there's also consolidation trades that could still be looked at -- trading two guys out, bringing one in," Lakers president of basketball operations Rob Pelinka said last month. "There's a number of ways that could be addressed."

Memphis Grizzlies
The Grizzlies have already made two roster decisions by waiving veteran D'Angelo Russell and former first-round pick Jordan Hawkins.

Memphis has 16 guaranteed contracts but needs to release two players because the $2.3 million salary of Jaylen Wells is set to become guaranteed on Oct. 19. Possible candidates include Kris Murray and Micah Peavy.

New York Knicks

New York loaded up on depth this summer by signing veterans Bruce Brown, Ochai Agbaji, Drew Eubanks, James Wiseman and Tony Bradley. But due to a self-imposed second apron hard cap, the Knicks are likely to keep just one of the five players despite having two open roster spots. They are currently $3.2 million below the second apron. Other options: Keep two players and then cut one during the season, or make a minor trade to clear out salary.

Other decisions to watch

The Hornets made a series of transactions in the offseason, trading Dorian Finney-Smith, Buddy Hield and waiving Ryan Nembhard. They have 16 players on standard contracts, including the non-guaranteed contract of veteran Pat Connaughton.
With Moussa Cisse's contract becoming guaranteed on Oct. 1, Dallas has 15 players on guaranteed deals. The Mavericks signed center Dwight Powell before training camp and need to waive the veteran or make another move to get their roster to 15 players.
The Warriors have a decision with their final two roster spots. They are hard-capped at the second apron and allowed to keep only three of these four players: Brandon Williams, Dalen Terry, Georges Niang and Charles Bassey. Terry, whose contract is not guaranteed, had a team-high 23 points in a preseason loss to the Trail Blazers on Oct. 7. Bassey ($1.4 million) and Niang's ($1.8 million) salaries are partially guaranteed, while Williams' salary increases from no protection to $1.4 million if he is not waived on the first day of the regular season.
The Clippers and Cam Christie agreed to move back his guaranteed date twice during the offseason. Now with a Thursday deadline looming, LA can guarantee the former second-round pick and waive a player on a guaranteed deal -- newly acquired Gradey Dick, for example -- or cut bait with Christie.
The four-for-one trade that sent Antetokounmpo to Miami has Milwaukee with 16 guaranteed contracts. Pete Nance's deal becomes guaranteed if he is not waived by Monday.

stories.headline: Every team's odds to win the 2026 World Series: Favored Brewers take 2-0 NLCS lead

stories.body:
The idea that the Los Angeles Dodgers might not win the World Series in 2026 is starting to become a reality, according to the odds. After losing title favorite status for the first time all season due to a Game 1 loss, the Dodgers also dropped Game 2 of the National League Championship Series and are out to +350 for the championship, their longest odds of the year.

The Milwaukee Brewers, meanwhile, extended their odds lead to +105 after coming into the NLCS with +300 World Series odds. Milwaukee was not expected to be a title contender coming into the season (according to bookmakers) as they started at a 14th-best 35-1.

Either Milwaukee or Los Angeles would likely be favored in the World Series against whichever team comes out of the American League. As of now, that would be the Cleveland Guardians, who stole a road Game 1 of the ALCS from the Tampa Bay Rays and improved their championship odds from +650 to +400. Tampa Bay fell from +330 to +475 with the loss.

stories.headline: NBA, WNBA campaign will remind fans of risks of betting on basketball
stories.summary: The NBA and WNBA are partnering with the National Council on Problem Gambling on a fan education campaign regarding the risks involved on betting or trading on basketball games.
stories.body:
As the season prepares to tip off, the NBA wants to remind fans that betting on basketball at sportsbooks and trading on prediction markets involves risk and should be done for entertainment, not to generate income.

The NBA and WNBA, in collaboration with the National Council on Problem Gambling, are launching a responsible gaming initiative this fall that will run on social and linear platforms. The campaign emphasizes that no matter how much one knows about basketball, their money is at stake.

"As the ways people engage with sports continue to evolve, it is important that fans understand the risks associated with putting money on sports outcomes," Scott Kaufman-Ross, NBA head of media distribution and partnerships, said in a release announcing the new campaign. "[We] want to help fans make informed decisions, understand the risk and, if they choose to bet, trade or anything similar, that they do so responsibly."

Colie Edison, the WNBA's chief growth officer, said helping fans make informed decisions is central to campaign.

"We can reach more fans with practical guidance on understanding financial risk, setting limits and recognizing when and where to find support," Edison said in the release.

The campaign points fans to responsible gaming education, resources to recognize problems and how to seek help, including references to gambling helplines.

"Awareness is an important first step in preventing gambling-related harm," Derek Longmeier, president of the NCPG board of directors, said in the release.

stories.headline: St. Louis unbeaten run up to 20 games, tying Red Bulls' MLS record
stories.summary: Carlo Holse's hat trick helped St. Louis City SC beat the LA Galaxy 6-2 on Sunday night to extend their unbeaten streak across all competitions to 20 games.
stories.body:
ST. LOUIS -- Carlo Holse's hat trick in the first 21 minutes -- the second hat trick in club history -- helped St. Louis City beat the LA Galaxy 6-2 on Sunday night to extend their unbeaten streak across all competitions to 20 games and tie the MLS record.

St. Louis, which is 13-0-5 in its last 18 regular-season games, tied the mark set when the New York Red Bulls went unbeaten in an MLS-record 20 consecutive games across all competitions in 2016.

Rafael Navarro converted from the penalty spot in the 45th minute, scored again in the 53rd and added two assists for St. Louis (14-6-8). Lukas MacNaughton scored on a diving header in the seventh minute of first-half stoppage time and Roman Bürki had five saves.

Holse opened the scoring in the second minute, added a goal in the seventh and skipped a shot inside the right post from the center of the area to make it 3-0 in the 21st minute to record the second-fastest hat trick in MLS history. Hany Mukhtar scored three goals for Nashville in the first 16 minutes of 5-1 win over Chicago on July 17, 2021.

The Galaxy's Kyōgo Furuhashi went off due to an apparent hamstring injury and was replaced in the 10th minute by João Klauss, whose goal in the 71st minute capped the scoring. Klauss, a 29-year-old midfielder in his first season with the Galaxy, had St. Louis City's first hat trick in a 3-3 tie with the Galaxy on June 14, 2025.

Robert Taylor scored in the 31st minute for the Galaxy (9-11-9).

St. Louis beat the Galaxy 3-1 on July 22 at Dignity Health Sports Park and hosts the Vancouver Whitecaps on Wednesday in a Western Conference top-of-table clash.

The Galaxy, who are clinging to the last playoff spot in the West, play the Portland Timbers at Dignity Health Sports Park on Wednesday. The Timbers are three points behind the Galaxy for ninth place -- the final playoff spot.

Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

stories.headline: Blackhawks' Connor Bedard 'happy' to finally make season debut vs. Penguins
stories.summary: Blackhawks captain Connor Bedard says he's "happy" to finally make his season debut Tuesday night against the Penguins following offseason shoulder surgery.
stories.body:
CHICAGO -- Chicago Blackhawks captain Connor Bedard is set for his season debut on Tuesday night against Pittsburgh.

Coach Jeff Blashill said Bedard is in the lineup for the matchup with Sidney Crosby and the Penguins. The 21-year-old center had surgery on his left shoulder on July 8.

"It's only been six games, but when you miss camp and you miss preseason it feels like a lot longer," Bedard said. "Just to be back with the guys and get to do what I love, it's exciting. Looking forward to getting back out there, for sure."

Chicago dropped five of its first six games without Bedard, who had a team-high 45 assists and 75 points last season. The Blackhawks have been outscored 26-12.

"We have to understand we're adding a good piece to the puzzle, but we can't expect him to put the puzzle together by himself," Blashill said.

Bedard is expected to play on the team's top line with Patrick Kane and rookie Roman Kantserov. Nick Lardis was assigned to Rockford of the AHL to make room for Bedard on the roster.

Bedard agreed to a $75 million, five-year contract in July. The No. 1 pick in the 2023 draft became the second-youngest captain in the history of the Original Six franchise on Sept. 15.

He got hurt while skating with a group of NHL players in western Canada this summer. After the operation, the team said he would be sidelined for approximately four months.

"You never really know how things are going to go," Bedard said. "I put a lot of time and effort into the rehab process to try and maybe come back a little earlier than I guess originally expected, but at the end of the day it's just when they felt comfortable. So it was safe for me to get back out there. But definitely happy that I didn't miss quite as many."

Bedard made his NHL debut against Crosby and the Penguins in 2023. He was heralded as the new face of the Blackhawks, and he won the Calder Trophy as the league's rookie of the year.

He missed 12 games last season after he hurt his right shoulder on Dec. 12. He wasn't allowed to take faceoffs after he returned, but he has no restrictions this year.

"It's nice. I mean, you want to just play your full game," Bedard said. "So just get back out there and you want to play as free as you can. It's nice that we had two practices for me to get into and feel some bumps and get into battles and stuff where it's not as controlled."

While Bedard is back, Frank Nazar will not play against the Penguins. The 22-year-old forward is finishing his two-game suspension for an illegal check on New York Islanders forward Bo Horvat on Thursday night.

stories.headline: Regulator: English football must address finances 'before it is too late'
stories.summary: The chair of the Independent Football Regulator says the English game must "act before it is too late" to tackle the financial dangers facing it.
stories.body:
The chair of the Independent Football Regulator says the English game must "act before it is too late" to tackle the financial dangers facing it.

The IFR published its draft 'State of the Game' report on Tuesday which found that while English football generated £9 billion ($11.9bn) in revenue last season, 94% of clubs in the top five divisions were loss-making.

Thirty-two clubs could not survive more than 30 days without owner funding, the report found, while 17 would be loss-making even if their players played for free.

IFR chair David Kogan said in the report's foreword that English club football was simultaneously the "richest, best and most deeply competitive in the world while also standing on the edge of financial disaster."

- Football Regulator chair will quit if politics interferes with any Man City investigation

The report forecasts total debt in English football would rise above £5bn ($6.6bn) by the end of this season, and that net transfer debt was approximately £3.4bn ($4.5bn), at a time when broadcast revenues are predicted to plateau or decline in the next cycle.

Kogan told the Press Association: "Everyone needs to take into account the fact that nothing is ever forever.

"We have to look at [the potential for broadcast revenues to fall] as a risk factor, and just make a judgement call, and actually also see what happens if the money does reduce.

"At the moment, the sun is shining. There's £9bn a year coming in. This is the very moment to address the issues of liquidity and losses and debt, before suddenly you see the money going backwards and it's too late.

"And our intention is to act before it's too late. And I believe, actually, the world of football wants that, and that's what we're going to do."

The IFR's action plan calls for reform to football's distribution mechanisms, finding that the average Premier League club earned 8.7 times more than the average Championship club in the 2024-25 season, compared to 2.7 times in 1992-93, the first season of the Premier League.

Kogan has been in the room with the Premier League and the EFL in recent months as they continue discussions over a 'New Deal' on funding and cost controls between the leagues.

"I have observed them dealing with issue after issue after issue, and reaching broad consensus on those issues, and inherently believe that the deal they're talking about now, if it comes off, might be effective in addressing some of the issues that we raise," he said.

One sticking point has always been parachute payments to clubs relegated from the Premier League. The report finds these are "distortive" and encourage overspending by Championship clubs, but also highlighted why they are necessary, finding that the clubs relegated from the top flight in 2024-25 saw a £70 million ($92.5m) average drop in revenue.

Kogan pointed out that the deal under discussion includes merit rakes, whereby a proportion of the solidarity funding from the Premier League to the EFL will be paid based on league position.

"Clubs in the top 10 positions of the Championship are going to receive more money," Kogan said.

"Clubs being relegated [who are] due parachute payments are going to get less money and the delta, which was 'that' [hands wide apart], is going to go to 'that' [hands closer together].

"Does that achieve everything that the EFL might have wanted three or four years ago? No. But it goes a long way towards addressing the issue. There are a lot of moving parts here and we hope they reach an agreement."

To tackle clubs' reliance on owner funding, clubs will be required as part of the IFR's licensing system to commit to an action plan setting out how they will meet the 'Appropriate Financial Resources' requirement by 2030.

- Enzo Maresca on Man City celebration at Anfield: 'What do you want us to do?'

- Steven Gerrard says Man City must be stripped of titles after guilty verdict: 'Make them suffer'

- Why did Man City fans bring inflatable bananas to Anfield?

Also, IFR chief executive Richard Monks said the regulator's team was alive as part of its licensing regime to what the report describes as "creative compliance" with existing competition rules, such as Chelsea selling hotels to companies linked to their ownership in order to meet Premier League financial rules.

"They understand what's going on, and crucially, they're a cynical bunch," he said.

"However a rule is phrased, a regulator should look at that rule and think, 'What do we think a club would do in that situation with that rule?' They will legitimately try and push the boundaries as far as they possibly can.

"[That is] perfectly reasonable. Your job as an effective regulator is to anticipate that, and therefore both write the rules but also supervise in a way that you manage those issues."

Football Supporters' Association chair Tom Greatrex called on the authorities to act on the IFR's findings and said that the report must be an "alarm call" which leads to "real and lasting change."

State of the Game report - action plan

The six-point action plan proposed by the report to improve English football's financial sustainability is as follows:

The distribution of revenue must be reformed, with changes focused on financial stability and not encourage imprudent spending. This reform should seek to "mitigate the financial impact of relegation from the Premier League" and "reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship."
Leagues, clubs and other stakeholders should take actions to reduce losses.
Action should be taken at the National League level to ensure football governance matches the risk within the game.
Clubs must improve how they manage financial risk. By 2030, the Football Governance Act requires clubs to hold 'Appropriate Financial Resources.' The IFR will require all clubs to commit to an action plan setting out how they will meet the 'Appropriate Financial Resources' requirement by 2030.
Clubs must show how they take fans' views into account.
Clubs must make progress on boardroom and senior executive diversity.

The IFR has also undertaken to produce an annual risk assessment, with the first to be published in the spring of 2028.

stories.headline: Formula 1 to return to Africa in 'early 2030s' as Rwanda race confirmed
stories.summary: Formula 1 is set to return to the African continent for the first time since 1993 after the sport confirmed a ten-year deal to host a race in Rwanda from "the early 2030s."
stories.body:
Formula 1 is set to return to the African continent for the first time since 1993 after the sport confirmed a 10-year deal to host a race in Rwanda from "the early 2030s."

After years of speculation about a return to the continent, F1 announced its plans for the "African Grand Prix" in a statement with Rwanda's president Paul Kagame on Tuesday.

The precise starting date of the new contract was not specified and is reliant on the construction of a purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 40 kilometres south of Rwanda's capital Kigali, which is set to be completed "early in the next decade."

The track, which will be built adjacent to the new Kigali International Airport, will be developed to the FIA Grade 1 standards required for F1 racing.

The last F1 race on the continent took place in South Africa in 1993 on the Kyalami circuit near Johannesburg, and Kagame described the sport's arrival in Rwanda as a moment that "belongs to Africa."

"For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement," Kagame said.

"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.

"This ten-year partnership is also an investment in Rwanda's future. The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."

F1's statement said the new circuit would "will be designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans."

It confirmed the circuit would be used for other international motorsport events during the rest of the year.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, who has long held an ambition for the sport to return to F1, said: "Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1. With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.

"Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact.

"I would like to thank His Excellency Paul Kagame, President of the Republic of Rwanda, the Government of Rwanda, the Rwanda Development Board, FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem and everyone whose dedication and collaboration have made this possible."

As recently as last weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton spoke of the importance of F1 returning to Africa in the coming years.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Rwanda F1 race: Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen welcome prospect

"I've always said that we need to have a Grand Prix in Africa," Hamilton said. "It is, for me, the most important continent and the most beautiful continent. We're on all the other continents but that one and there should be no reason for it.

"It's something I've been pushing for in the background and Stefano's been amazing -- he's flown to Africa so many times over the last couple of years speaking to lots of different people and so I hope he has some news for me soon."

The grand prix in Rwanda will be added to an already packed F1 calendar, which is currently maxed out with the sport's self-imposed limit of 24 rounds per season.

Races in Portugal and Türkiye's are set to return to the schedule next year, following on from the addition of a new venue in Madrid this year.

stories.headline: Ranking every AFL free agent by the impact they'll have at their new club
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL free agency period is now complete. We've ranked every move that has been made, factoring in positional needs and their likely impact for season 2027.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL free agency period is now complete, with seven players finding new clubs either as restricted or unrestricted free agents.

We've ranked every move that has been made, factoring in positional needs and their likely impact for season 2027 (not the rest of their career). So, who will be the biggest needle mover of the bunch in the immediate future?

7. Kieren Briggs
This is absolutely no criticism of Kieren Briggs, but there really aren't many players in the competition (if any) that could be dropped into the Tigers in 2027 and be serious needle movers. Remember, Richmond has won just 10 games across the last three seasons and is widely expected to finish in the bottom four once again next year. Tigers skipper Toby Nankervis will remain the club's primary ruck in the immediate future, but the arrival of Briggs will allow for a new-look one-two punch. The former Giant is one of the best hitout-to-advantage rucks in the game and an elite clearance winner. At 27 years of age, and with Nankervis now 32, Briggs' impact will likely be felt in the years beyond 2027.

6. Jordon Butts
Key defensive stocks have been a concern for the Bulldogs in recent years, so the signing of Jordon Butts will be a welcomed addition for the club. Butts makes the move after eight seasons and 94 games with the Crows, but he's managed just 10 and nine games in 2025 and 2026. Throughout different parts of the last couple of years, he's struggled with unlucky injuries; in 2025 it was a collapsed lung, and this year he battled concussion and a fractured foot. With the continued strong form of Josh Worrell and Mark Keane, and emergence of Josh Borlase at the Crows, a move to the Bulldogs makes sense for both the 26-year-old Butts and the Dogs.

5. Joel Amartey
The Blues landed key forward support for Harry McKay in the form of Joel Amartey, who crosses from the Swans as an unrestricted free agent. It's a shrewd acquisition for Carlton, and the club will be hopeful he can be an upgrade on both Brodie Kemp and Mitch McGovern. Amartey is coming off a season at Sydney in which he booted 28 goals from 15 games and averaged three marks per game. In 2024 he enjoyed a career-best 43-goal campaign, including a bag of nine against the Crows. Amartey is just 27 years of age and should only really be coming into his prime as a key position player in the AFL. Could surprise a few in 2027.

4. Toby Greene
Another year, another major coup for the Cats. Is anyone surprised?! Former Giants captain Toby Greene joins Geelong as an unrestricted free agent while GWS has to make do with second-round compensation. We all know Greene has been a high-impact player throughout his 15-year career and he will add a whole new dynamic to the Cats' forward line, one that features former Giants teammate and close friend Jeremy Cameron. In 2026, Greene kicked 34 goals -- his lowest return in a season since his injury-interrupted 2020 campaign -- but did amass over 20 disposals per game. If anyone wanted to argue he deserves the top spot on this list I wouldn't scoff, but it's not as if the Cats had trouble scoring in 2026...

3. Ben King
It may have been a move that surprised few, but it's one -- along with the signing of Zach Merrett, of course -- that will have Hawks fans believing a premiership is possible in 2027. For a fair chunk of the 2026 season, King looked to be the Coleman Medal winner. Gold Coast's capitulation didn't help his chances, though he still finished the home and away season with 60 goals to his name -- the third consecutive year he's managed 55+ goals. King will partner veteran Jack Gunston and dynamo Nick Watson in what now looks to be one of the most dangerous forward lines in the game.

2. Lachie Neale
The Lachie Neale-Brisbane Lions era is over, with the two-time Brownlow Medal winner joining Collingwood as an unrestricted free agent and partnering reigning Brownlow winner Nick Daicos in a new-look Magpies midfield. Neale might be 33 years of age and on the downturn of his decorated career, but he still averaged 29 disposals, 12.5 contested possessions, and six clearances per outing in 2026 and figures to be a major contributor next season in a Collingwood engine room that's often lacked depth and firepower. Even if the Magpies receive 80-85% of this season's production from Neale, he'll be difficult to top as the most impactful free agent of the year.

1. Zak Butters
The most sought after man in football made the decision to sign with the Bulldogs during free agency. Former Power star Zak Butters joins the club as a top five player in the game, and at age 26, you can certainly make the argument he's only at the beginning of his prime. Butters will partner Western Bulldogs skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards in what's easily the most impressive and dynamic three-pronged midfield in the competition. He offers a real point of difference, too, with his electric pace and the ability to break lines two eye-catching features that have seen him ascend to footy superstardom.

stories.headline: New Zealand Rugby launches legal action against ARLC over 'Chiefs' name
stories.summary: The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.
stories.body:
The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.

NZR on Thursday said it had been left with no choice but to launch legal proceedings against the ARLC, who has sought to adopt the name for its Papua New Guinea expansion franchise.

The PNG Chiefs are due to join the NRL in 2028 and have already signed a raft of players, including code-hoppers Zac Lomaz and Joey Manu, but they may yet have to undergo a chanGe of name if NZR gets its way.

The Chiefs' Super Rugby franchise has existed since 1996, with NZR claiming the introduction of the PNG Chiefs would result in "significant confusion and damage" should they be allowed to compete under the name from 2028.

"New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has today moved to protect the Chiefs brand and is filing proceedings in the High Court of New Zealand against the decision by the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) to launch a new NRL side using "Chiefs" in its name," an NZR statement read.  

"NZR is seeking both an interim and final injunction which stops the use of the names 'PNG Chiefs', 'Chiefs' or any other similar names in New Zealand.   

"The Chiefs have competed as a professional rugby team in Super Rugby since 1996 and over those 30 years, have built a strong identity and fanbase across New Zealand, Australia and internationally.  

"In New Zealand, NZR owns both the trademark rights for the word Chiefs and the Chiefs logo and since 1998, NZR has also held trademark protection for the Chiefs logo in Australia."

NZR claims it had tried to engage with the ARLC in an attempt to find a resolution, yet the commission was now intent on proceeding with the official launch of the PNG Chiefs on Oct. 21.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said. "We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand.   

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific. We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."  

The Chiefs won two Super Rugby titles in back-to-back seasons in 2012 and 2013, and were runners-up in Super Rugby Pacific this season after suffering a crushing defeat by the Hurricanes in the decider.

The Hamilton-based team has produced countless All Blacks since its inception, with Saturday's run-on team to face the Wallabies featuring six players from the franchise.

"Here in New Zealand, when people hear 'the Chiefs', they think of this club and this region. The identity carries significant cultural meaning and connection to the region and its people, we know it means a great deal to our players and coaches past and present, fans and supporters here and around the world," Chiefs CEO Simon Graafhuis said.   

"Teams in different sports and markets can exist alongside one another with the same name, but the issue here is the similarity of our sports competing in the same market, for the same fans, in overlapping windows."  

However, ARLC executive chairman Peter V'Landys later issued a stinging rebuke, insisting he would vigorously defend PNG's right to use the Chiefs as its team name.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval. The NSW Blues had been the Blues for in excess of 50 years before that," he said.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

No date has yet been slated for the hearing in New Zealand's High Court.
